prompt:
Let $a,b$ and $c$ be positive real numbers such that $a+b+c=1$. Show that
$$\left(\frac1a+\frac1{bc}\right)\left(\frac1b+\frac1{ca}\right)\left(\frac1c+\frac1{ab}\right)\ge1728 .$$
answer: $\frac1a+\frac1{bc}=\frac{(a+b)(a+c)}{abc}$, so the product is $\frac{[(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)]^2}{(abc)^3}\ge\frac{64}{abc}\ge64\cdot27=1728$. Equality holds at $a=b=c=\frac13$.

solutions.title: AM-GM with four terms (official)
solutions.body:
Split $\frac1{bc}$ into three equal parts and apply AM-GM to four numbers:
$$\frac1a+\frac1{bc}=\frac1a+\frac1{3bc}+\frac1{3bc}+\frac1{3bc}\ge4\sqrt[4]{\frac1{27\,a\,b^3c^3}} .$$
Multiplying the three analogous inequalities,
$$\prod\Big(\frac1a+\frac1{bc}\Big)\ge\frac{64}{\sqrt[4]{27^3\,a^7b^7c^7}}=\frac{64}{\sqrt[4]{3^9(abc)^7}} .$$
By AM-GM, $abc\le\left(\frac{a+b+c}3\right)^3=3^{-3}$. Hence the right side is at least
$$\frac{64}{\sqrt[4]{3^9\cdot3^{-21}}}=64\cdot3^{3}=1728 .$$
Equality holds for $a=b=c=\frac13$. ∎

solutions.title: Factor using $a+b+c=1$
solutions.body:
Since $a+b+c=1$,
$$\frac1a+\frac1{bc}=\frac{bc+a}{abc}=\frac{bc+a(a+b+c)}{abc}=\frac{(a+b)(a+c)}{abc}.$$
Hence
$$\prod\Big(\frac1a+\frac1{bc}\Big)=\frac{\big[(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)\big]^2}{(abc)^3}.$$
By AM-GM, $a+b\ge2\sqrt{ab}$ etc., so $(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)\ge8abc$. Also $abc\le\frac1{27}$. Therefore
$$\prod\Big(\frac1a+\frac1{bc}\Big)\ge\frac{64(abc)^2}{(abc)^3}=\frac{64}{abc}\ge64\cdot27=1728 .\ ∎$$

prompt: Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal P(X)$ be the set of all subsets of $X$. Let $\mu\colon\mathcal P(X)\to\mathcal P(X)$ be a map with the property that $\mu(A\cup B)=\mu(A)\cup\mu(B)$ whenever $A$ and $B$ are disjoint subsets of $X$. Prove that there exists a set $F\subset X$ such that $\mu(F)=F$.
answer: $\mu$ is monotone. Then $F=\bigcap\{A:\mu(A)\subset A\}$ is a fixed point (Knaster–Tarski).

solutions.title: Monotonicity and the Knaster–Tarski argument
solutions.body:
**$\mu$ is monotone.** If $A\subset B$, then $B=A\cup(B\setminus A)$ is a disjoint union, so
$$\mu(B)=\mu(A)\cup\mu(B\setminus A)\supset\mu(A).$$

**The fixed point.** Let $\mathcal F=\{A\subset X:\mu(A)\subset A\}$. It is nonempty because $X\in\mathcal F$. Put $F=\bigcap_{A\in\mathcal F}A$.

* For every $A\in\mathcal F$ we have $F\subset A$, so $\mu(F)\subset\mu(A)\subset A$ by monotonicity. Intersecting over all $A\in\mathcal F$ gives $\mu(F)\subset F$.
* Applying monotonicity to $\mu(F)\subset F$ gives $\mu(\mu(F))\subset\mu(F)$, so $\mu(F)\in\mathcal F$. Hence $F\subset\mu(F)$.

Both inclusions give $\mu(F)=F$. ∎

solutions.title: The dual construction
solutions.body:
With $\mu$ monotone as above, we can also start from below. Let $\mathcal G=\{A:A\subset\mu(A)\}$; it contains $\emptyset$. Put $G=\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal G}A$.

* For $A\in\mathcal G$, $A\subset\mu(A)\subset\mu(G)$, so $G\subset\mu(G)$.
* Then $\mu(G)\subset\mu(\mu(G))$, so $\mu(G)\in\mathcal G$ and $\mu(G)\subset G$.

Hence $\mu(G)=G$ is also a fixed point; it is the largest one, while $F$ above is the smallest. ∎

prompt:
For $n\ge3$ find the eigenvalues (with their multiplicities) of the $n\times n$ matrix
$$\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1&0&0&0&\cdots&\cdots&0&0\\0&2&0&1&0&0&\cdots&\cdots&0&0\\1&0&2&0&1&0&\cdots&\cdots&0&0\\0&1&0&2&0&1&\cdots&\cdots&0&0\\0&0&1&0&2&0&\cdots&\cdots&0&0\\0&0&0&1&0&2&\cdots&\cdots&0&0\\\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&&\vdots&\vdots\\\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\0&0&0&0&0&0&\cdots&\cdots&2&0\\0&0&0&0&0&0&\cdots&\cdots&0&1\end{bmatrix}.$$
answer: $4\cos^2\frac{k\pi}{n+1}$ for $k=1,\dots,n$. For $1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ these are distinct and each has multiplicity $2$; for odd $n$ there is in addition the simple eigenvalue $0$ (from $k=\frac{n+1}2$). The matrix is $B^2$ with $B$ the path adjacency matrix.

solutions.title: Square of the path adjacency matrix
solutions.body:
Let $B$ be the $n\times n$ matrix with $1$ on the first super- and sub-diagonal and $0$ elsewhere (the adjacency matrix of a path). The entry $(B^2)_{ij}$ counts walks of length $2$ from $i$ to $j$:
* it equals $1$ for $i=j\in\{1,n\}$;
* it equals $2$ for $1<i=j<n$;
* it equals $1$ for $|i-j|=2$;
* it equals $0$ otherwise.

So the given matrix is $A=B^2$.

**Eigenvectors of $B$.** For $k=1,\dots,n$ let $\theta_k=\frac{k\pi}{n+1}$ and $v_k=\big(\sin\theta_k,\sin2\theta_k,\dots,\sin n\theta_k\big)^T$. Since $\sin0=\sin(n+1)\theta_k=0$,
$$(Bv_k)_j=\sin(j-1)\theta_k+\sin(j+1)\theta_k=2\cos\theta_k\,\sin j\theta_k\qquad(1\le j\le n).$$
So $Bv_k=2\cos\theta_k\,v_k$, and $v_k\ne0$ since $\sin\theta_k\ne0$. The $n$ numbers $2\cos\theta_k$ are distinct because $0<\theta_1<\dots<\theta_n<\pi$. Hence $v_1,\dots,v_n$ is an eigenbasis.

**Eigenvalues of $A$.** In the same basis, $Av_k=B^2v_k=4\cos^2\theta_k\,v_k$. So $A$ is diagonalizable with eigenvalues $4\cos^2\frac{k\pi}{n+1}$, $k=1,\dots,n$, counted with multiplicity. Now $\cos^2\theta_k=\cos^2\theta_l$ iff $l=k$ or $l=n+1-k$.

**Answer:**
* For $k=1,\dots,\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ the eigenvalue $4\cos^2\frac{k\pi}{n+1}$ has multiplicity $2$.
* If $n$ is odd, there is also the eigenvalue $4\cos^2\frac\pi2=0$ with multiplicity $1$.

(Example: $n=5$ gives $3,3,1,1,0$.) ∎

solutions.title: Characteristic polynomial of $B$ (official route)
solutions.body:
Expanding $S_n(\lambda)=\det(\lambda I-B)$ along the last row gives the recurrence
$$S_n=\lambda S_{n-1}-S_{n-2},\qquad S_1=\lambda,\ S_2=\lambda^2-1 .$$
This is the recurrence of the Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind, so $S_n(\lambda)=U_n(\lambda/2)$. With $\lambda=2\cos\theta$, $\theta\in(0,\pi)$, we get $S_n(\lambda)=\frac{\sin(n+1)\theta}{\sin\theta}$. This vanishes exactly at $\theta=\frac{k\pi}{n+1}$, $k=1,\dots,n$, which gives $n$ distinct roots $2\cos\frac{k\pi}{n+1}$. Since $S_n$ has degree $n$, these are all the eigenvalues of $B$, each simple.

$B$ is real symmetric, hence orthogonally diagonalizable, $B=U\Lambda U^T$. Then $A=B^2=U\Lambda^2U^T$ has eigenvalues $4\cos^2\frac{k\pi}{n+1}$, $k=1,\dots,n$, with multiplicities as in the first solution. ∎

prompt:
Let $f\colon[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be a continuously differentiable function satisfying
$$f(x)=\int_{x-1}^xf(t)\,dt$$
for all $x\ge1$. Show that $f$ has bounded variation on $[1,\infty)$, i.e.
$$\int_1^\infty|f'(x)|\,dx<\infty .$$
answer: For $x\ge1$, $g=f'$ satisfies $g(x)=\int_{x-1}^xg$ and $\int_{x-1}^x(t-x+1)g(t)\,dt=0$. Hence $|g(x)|\le\frac12\max_{[x-1,x]}|g|$, the maxima of $|f'|$ on $[n,n+1]$ decay geometrically, and $\int_1^\infty|f'|<\infty$.

solutions.title: Two identities for $f'$ and a contraction
solutions.body:
Let $g=f'$, which is continuous on $[0,\infty)$. Fix $x\ge1$.

**Identity 1.** Differentiating $f(x)=\int_{x-1}^xf$ (the right side is differentiable since $f$ is continuous) gives
$$g(x)=f(x)-f(x-1)=\int_{x-1}^xg(t)\,dt\qquad(x\ge1).$$

**Identity 2.** Integrate by parts:
$$\int_{x-1}^x(t-x+1)\,g(t)\,dt=\Big[(t-x+1)f(t)\Big]_{t=x-1}^{t=x}-\int_{x-1}^xf(t)\,dt=f(x)-f(x)=0 .$$

**Contraction.** Let $M(x)=\max_{[x-1,x]}|g|$. Combining the two identities,
$$g(x)=\int_{x-1}^xg(t)\,dt-2\int_{x-1}^x(t-x+1)g(t)\,dt=\int_{x-1}^x\big(1-2(t-x+1)\big)g(t)\,dt .$$
Hence
$$|g(x)|\le M(x)\int_0^1|1-2s|\,ds=\tfrac12M(x).\tag{$*$}$$

**Geometric decay.** Let $M_n=\max_{[n,n+1]}|g|$ for $n\ge0$. For $n\ge1$ and $x\in[n,n+1]$, $(*)$ gives $|g(x)|\le\frac12\max(M_{n-1},M_n)$.
* If $M_n>M_{n-1}$, choose $x$ with $|g(x)|=M_n$. Then $M_n\le\frac12M_n$, so $M_n=0\le M_{n-1}$, a contradiction.
* Hence $M_n\le M_{n-1}$, and then $M_n\le\frac12M_{n-1}$.

So $M_n\le2^{-n}M_0$ and
$$\int_1^\infty|f'(x)|\,dx=\sum_{n\ge1}\int_n^{n+1}|g|\le\sum_{n\ge1}2^{-n}M_0=M_0<\infty .\ ∎$$

*Remarks.*
* Choosing the weight optimally, $\min_\lambda\int_0^1|1-\lambda s|\,ds=\sqrt2-1$, improves the constant $\frac12$ to $\sqrt2-1$.
* The official solution argues differently. It shows that the maximum $A_n$ and minimum $B_n$ of $f$ on $[n,n+1]$ are monotone, then proves the quantitative bound $d_{n+2}\le d_n-\frac{d_n^5}{64d_{n-1}^4}$ for $d_n=A_n-B_n$. From this, $d_{n+2}/d_{n-2}\le\frac{63}{64}$ and $\sum d_n<\infty$; finally $|f'|\le d_{n-1}$ on $[n,n+1]$ because $f'(x)=f(x)-f(x-1)$.
